title: "Effective sample size"

Suppose we save 1,000 draws, but each value is very similar to the one before
it. Those draws still contribute information, though they will generally not
estimate a posterior mean as precisely as 1,000 independent draws. We want to
express the loss in the same units as the independent Monte Carlo calculation.

The **effective sample size (ESS)** is the number of independent posterior
draws that would give approximately the same Monte Carlo precision for a
particular summary. If 1,000 dependent draws give the same variance for a
posterior-mean estimate as 400 independent draws, their ESS for that estimate
is about 400.

Why does dependence change the variance of an average? Recall from the
[variance--covariance decomposition](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd)
that the variance of a sum includes both variances and covariances. Independent
draws make the covariance terms zero. Markov-chain draws generally leave some
of them behind. We will first see this with three draws, then collect the same
terms using the autocorrelations defined on the [preceding page](autocorrelation.qmd).

## From autocorrelation to ESS

For three identically distributed draws,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\left[\frac{\Theta_1+\Theta_2+\Theta_3}{3}\right]
&=
\frac19\big(
\operatorname{Var}[\Theta_1]
+\operatorname{Var}[\Theta_2]
+\operatorname{Var}[\Theta_3]\\
&\quad
+2\operatorname{Cov}[\Theta_1,\Theta_2]
+2\operatorname{Cov}[\Theta_1,\Theta_3]
+2\operatorname{Cov}[\Theta_2,\Theta_3]
\big).
\end{aligned}
$$

If the three draws are independent and each has variance $\sigma^2$, only the
first three terms remain and the average has variance $\sigma^2/3$. Positive
covariances make it larger. The general formula below performs the same
accounting for $S$ draws and groups covariance terms by how many iterations
separate them.

For a stationary scalar sequence of $S$ draws,

$$
\operatorname{ESS}
\approx
\frac{S}{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t}.
$$

This denominator follows from the variance of a correlated average. If every draw has variance $\sigma^2$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[\overline\Theta_S]
&=
\frac{1}{S^2}
\left[
S\sigma^2
+2\sum_{t=1}^{S-1}(S-t)\sigma^2\rho_t
\right]\\
&\approx
\frac{\sigma^2}{S}
\left(1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Equating this expression with the independent-draw variance $\sigma^2/\operatorname{ESS}$ gives the displayed approximation.

The denominator is the integrated autocorrelation time. Positive dependence increases it and reduces ESS; negative dependence can make ESS exceed the raw draw count for some summaries.

For a function $g(\mu,\lambda)$ with posterior standard deviation $\sigma_g$,

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}
\approx
\frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ESS}}}.
$$

Repeating the simulation while holding the observed data and posterior fixed would change the numerical estimate of the posterior mean. MCSE describes that run-to-run numerical variation. Posterior uncertainty instead varies parameter values under the fitted posterior while conditioning on the observed data.

## passage-level Student-t model effective sample sizes

The code computes a textbook positive-sequence estimate for chain one's $\mu$ draws, then obtains modern four-chain bulk and tail ESS from `posterior`.

For the one-chain calculation, we stop at the first nonpositive estimated autocorrelation because noisy long-lag estimates can otherwise dominate the sum. This simple truncation uses only one chain and does not stabilize the paired autocorrelation sequence. Modern estimators instead combine chains and truncate paired sums only after the sequence stops behaving monotonically and positively. Bulk ESS additionally rank-normalizes draws; tail ESS targets indicator-like tail quantities. Thus these values address different summaries and need not match the one-chain value.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-effective-sample-size
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
production <- posterior::subset_draws(
  cache$production_draws,
  variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)
draws <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(production))
mu_chain_one <- draws$mu[draws$.chain == 1L]
acf_values <- as.numeric(acf(mu_chain_one, lag.max = 40L,
                             plot = FALSE, demean = TRUE)$acf)[-1]
first_nonpositive <- which(acf_values <= 0)
if (length(first_nonpositive)) {
  keep <- first_nonpositive[1] - 1L
  acf_values <- if (keep > 0L) acf_values[seq_len(keep)] else numeric(0)
}
integrated_time <- 1 + 2 * sum(acf_values)
textbook_ess <- length(mu_chain_one) / integrated_time

mu_draws <- posterior::subset_draws(production, variable = "mu")
sigma_draws <- posterior::subset_draws(production, variable = "sigma")
ess_summary <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("chain-one textbook mu", "four-chain bulk mu",
               "four-chain tail mu", "four-chain bulk sigma",
               "four-chain tail sigma"),
  ess = c(
    textbook_ess,
    posterior::ess_bulk(mu_draws),
    posterior::ess_tail(mu_draws),
    posterior::ess_bulk(sigma_draws),
    posterior::ess_tail(sigma_draws)
  )
)
posterior_sd_mu <- sd(draws$mu)
mcse_mu <- posterior::mcse_mean(mu_draws)

stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L, length(mu_chain_one) == 1000L,
          min(ess_summary$ess) > 100L)
ess_summary
```

The one-chain textbook value is `r round(textbook_ess)`. The modern bulk ESS for $\mu$ is `r round(posterior::ess_bulk(mu_draws))`, while its tail ESS is `r round(posterior::ess_tail(mu_draws))`. These are different estimators applied to different collections of draws, so their difference is not a disagreement.

The posterior standard deviation of $\mu$ is `r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_sd_mu)`, whereas the estimated MCSE of its posterior mean is `r sprintf("%.6f", mcse_mu)`. This separation is the point of ESS.

Bulk ESS uses rank-normalized draws and is useful for location summaries. Tail ESS targets information relevant to the 5% and 95% quantiles. A chain can move adequately through the center but rarely reach a tail, so the appropriate diagnostic depends on the reported summary.

ESS translates dependence among simulation draws into an independent-draw count with comparable numerical precision. Running longer can increase this count and reduce MCSE while leaving the 55 observed passage summaries unchanged. Additional passages, positions, or readers would require new empirical observations and could change the posterior itself.

## Recap and forward link

1. Correlated-average variance produces the integrated-autocorrelation-time denominator.
2. ESS is quantity specific; bulk and tail summaries can differ.
3. Autocorrelation truncation is needed because long-lag estimates become noisy.
4. ESS counts computational information, not linguistic observations.

The [divergence page](divergent-transitions.qmd#energy-error-and-geometry) next checks whether HMC integration fails in localized target regions.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does positive autocorrelation tend to reduce ESS?
2. Why can bulk and tail ESS differ?
3. Which quantity changes when the sampler runs longer: posterior spread or MCSE?
4. Why is passage-level Student-t model ESS not a linguistic sample size?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Positive autocorrelations increase the integrated autocorrelation time in the denominator of ESS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Movement can be efficient near the posterior center but slow in the tails, and the two diagnostics target different summaries of the draws. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. MCSE can decrease as the run grows; posterior spread remains a property of the fixed posterior target. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. passage-level Student-t model ESS counts information in simulated posterior draws, not Provo passages, word positions, readers, or any other linguistic unit. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
